writingIdeas.viewpoint: A few close friends can be more valuable than a large social circle.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: The quality of friendships often matters more than the number of people someone knows.
writingIdeas.argument: Close friendships require time, repeated contact and a willingness to be honest. Because trust develops gradually, a small number of friends may understand someone better than dozens of casual contacts. They can notice changes in behaviour and offer advice based on long experience. This depth is especially valuable during illness, failure or loneliness. A broad network is useful, but it does not automatically provide the security of a trusted friendship.

writingIdeas.viewpoint: Schools can help children develop friendship skills.
writingIdeas.topicSentence: Social skills should be treated as part of children’s development rather than left entirely to chance.
writingIdeas.argument: Children do not always know how to join a group, handle rejection or repair a disagreement. Teachers can model respectful language and create activities that require cooperation with different classmates. This is not the same as choosing friends for children; it gives them tools for forming healthier relationships. It may also help isolated pupils participate without being singled out. Basic friendship skills can therefore improve both well-being and the classroom environment.

speaking.question: Do you prefer having a few close friends or a large group of friends?
speaking.answer: I prefer a few close friends. I enjoy meeting new people, but I don’t have the time or energy to maintain dozens of close relationships. With my closest friends, I can talk openly and I don’t need to explain every bit of background. A larger group is fun for an event, whereas a small circle is better when I actually need support.

speaking.question: What do you usually do when you meet your friends?
speaking.answer: Most of the time, we choose somewhere quiet to eat and catch up. We used to go to the cinema quite often, but then we realised we spent the whole evening without speaking. Now we might take a walk after dinner or play a simple board game. The activity isn’t especially important; it just gives us time to talk.

reading.title: Why Some Friendships Survive Distance
paragraphs: Moving away once placed a severe limit on friendship. Letters were slow, international calls were expensive, and people who left a town could disappear from everyday life. Digital communication has removed much of that practical difficulty. A message can cross continents instantly, yet many long-distance friendships still fade. The availability of contact, it seems, is different from the motivation to maintain it.

Friendship is supported by what social researchers sometimes call repeated low-cost interaction. Classmates and colleagues see one another without arranging every meeting. They exchange small pieces of information, share minor frustrations and gradually build a detailed picture of each other’s lives. After one person moves, this background contact vanishes. Scheduled video calls may be longer, but they cannot always reproduce the ordinary moments that once kept both friends familiar with changing routines.

Some pairs adapt by lowering the pressure surrounding communication. Instead of expecting an hour-long conversation, they send photographs, short recordings or links that reflect a shared interest. These small signals say that the other person remains part of daily thought. Importantly, successful friends do not treat every delayed reply as rejection. Workload, time differences and family duties can interrupt communication without weakening affection.

Distance can even reveal which friendships are based on convenience and which have a stronger foundation. Friends who share trust and a history of mutual support may resume a conversation after months with little discomfort. Others discover that a common workplace or neighbourhood was doing most of the work. Neither outcome makes the earlier friendship false. Relationships serve different purposes at different stages, and maintaining every connection indefinitely may be neither possible nor desirable.

Long-distance friendships also need some expectation of a future meeting, even if the date remains uncertain. Digital contact maintains awareness, but shared physical experiences supply new memories and prevent the relationship from depending entirely on the past. When meetings are rare, ordinary activities such as cooking together may be more restorative than an ambitious programme of sightseeing.
